modules.title: CompTIA Core Stack: A+, Network+, Security+
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 1 of IL-09, the Adaptive Certification Command. I'm your instructor, and this is where the certification campaign begins: the CompTIA core stack — A+, Network+, Security+ — sequenced so the knowledge compounds and the stackable credentials (CIOS, then CSIS) fall out of the order automatically. We study by domain weight, not by the order the objectives are printed: A+ Core 1's Hardware (25%) and Hardware/Network Troubleshooting (28%) come first because more than half the exam lives there. Security+ SY0-701 is taught as what it is — a security-operations exam, with its 28% Operations domain at the center. Every drill here pairs official exam objectives with original practice material: PBQ-style labs, subnetting sprints, and the six-step troubleshooting methodology applied until it's reflex.
objectives: Map the A+ Core 1/Core 2 domains by weight and study the heavy domains first.
Reach subnetting fluency: /24 math in your head, VLSM on paper, troubleshooting by elimination.
Apply the six-step troubleshooting methodology to every PBQ-style scenario.
Internalize the Security+ domains with emphasis on Security Operations (28%).
Sequence A+ → Network+ → Security+ to earn CIOS then CSIS stackables.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **A+ Core 1 (220-1201)** — Hardware, networking, mobile devices, virtualization/cloud concepts, and hardware/network troubleshooting. Domain weights: Hardware 25%, Hardware & Network Troubleshooting 28% — more than half the exam. Study order follows weight, not the objectives list order.
- **A+ Core 2 (220-1202)** — Operating systems, security concepts, software troubleshooting, and operational procedures. Domain weights: Operating Systems 31%, Security 25%. Windows/macOS/Linux OS features lead the study order.
- **PBQ** — Performance-Based Question. These open the CompTIA exams and test applied skill in simulated environments. Do them first while fresh; flag and return if one eats more than ~4 minutes. Never leave one blank.
- **Six-step troubleshooting methodology** — The CompTIA-prescribed sequence: 1) Identify the problem, 2) Establish a theory of probable cause, 3) Test the theory, 4) Establish a plan of action, 5) Implement the solution, 6) Verify functionality and document. Memorize it in order — CompTIA asks which step comes next.
- **Network+ N10-009** — The connective-tissue exam. Domain weights: Networking Concepts 23%, Implementation 20%, Operations 19%, Security 14%, Troubleshooting 24%. Troubleshooting is the single largest domain.
- **Subnetting** — Trainable arithmetic: given 192.168.10.0/26, produce network/broadcast/usable range in under 60 seconds. 2^(32−26) − 2 = 62 usable hosts. On the exam, always isolate by OSI layer — physical first, then data link, then up the stack.
- **DHCP DORA** — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the four-step DHCP handshake. Know it as a behavior, not a memorized acronym.
- **DNS recursion vs iteration** — A recursive resolver walks the hierarchy on the client's behalf; iterative queries return referrals and let the client keep walking. Exam questions test which one a given server performs.
- **TCP three-way handshake** — SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, and know what each flag means — this is the *why* behind protocol questions.
- **Security+ SY0-701** — Reorganized around security operations. Domain weights: General Security Concepts 12%, Threats/Vulnerabilities/Mitigations 22%, Security Architecture 18%, Security Operations 28%, Security Program Management 20%. The largest domain is incident response, digital forensics basics, SIEM/log analysis, and vulnerability management workflow.
- **Log reading** — Timestamps, source/destination, action: most Security Operations questions are log-reading in disguise. Practice reading firewall, IDS, and endpoint logs as narratives.
- **Threat classification** — Classify first, then match the control: malware types, social engineering vectors, attack surfaces.
- **Zero trust** — Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach — the design philosophy behind Security+ architecture questions, alongside segmentation and cloud models.
- **Risk vocabulary** — Risk appetite, risk tolerance, risk register: the governance vocabulary of the 20% Program Management domain.
- **CIOS** — CompTIA IT Operations Specialist stackable: earned with A+ + Network+.
- **CSIS** — CompTIA Secure Infrastructure Specialist stackable: earned with A+ + Network+ + Security+. The booking order A+ → Network+ → Security+ earns CIOS then CSIS with no wasted exams.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the domain-weighted study loop — the procedure you'll repeat for every exam in this campaign. It replaces reading-and-hoping with measurable readiness.

1. **Pull the official objectives.** Download the current objectives PDF from comptia.org for the exact exam series you're booking (e.g., 220-1201, N10-009, SY0-701). Third-party summaries older than the current series are study poison.
2. **Rank domains by weight.** Write each domain and its percentage on one page. Your study hours follow weight: A+ Core 1's Hardware + Troubleshooting (53%) gets the bulk; Security+'s Operations (28%) is your largest single investment.
3. **Build the heaviest-domain first.** Attack the heaviest domain before touching anything else. For A+ Core 1 that means hardware install/configure depth; for Security+ it means reading log lines and working incident-response scenarios.
4. **Run the daily drill.** Subnetting sprint (network/broadcast/usable in under 60 seconds), six-step methodology recitation, one PBQ-style lab per sitting. Reflexes are trained, not read.
5. **Do PBQs first on exam day.** Open with the performance-based questions while your working memory is fresh. If one exceeds ~4 minutes, flag it and return — a stalled PBQ can eat the time two multiple-choice questions would earn.
6. **Apply the methodology to every scenario question.** Before choosing an answer, name the step: are you identifying, theorizing, or testing? CompTIA scenario questions reward the disciplined sequence.
7. **Pass the readiness gate before booking.** A domain-weighted practice set at 80%+ across two sittings is the gate. No booking until the gate is green — exam fees are too expensive to spend on hope.

modules.title: CompTIA Security Track: CySA+, PenTest+, SecurityX
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 2 of IL-09, the Adaptive Certification Command. I'm your instructor, and this module is the cybersecurity pathway: CySA+ (defend — security operations, vulnerability management, incident response), PenTest+ (attack — engagement management through post-exploitation), and SecurityX (architect — GRC, architecture, engineering at the expert tier). CySA+ thinks in workflows, not definitions: the vulnerability-management lifecycle and the incident-response phases are what get tested. PenTest+ punishes cowboys — scoping and rules of engagement come first, always, and reporting is 17% of the exam and the most under-studied domain in it. SecurityX is scenario-based and pass/fail: enterprise situations with competing constraints, where the right answer balances the constraint set rather than the ideal. Stackables CSAE/CSIE cap the track.
objectives: Run the CySA+ domains by weight: security operations first, then vulnerability management, then incident response.
Plan a PenTest+ engagement end-to-end: scoping, recon, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting.
Reason about SecurityX architecture scenarios: GRC constraints shaping engineering choices.
Earn the stackables in order: CSAP (Security+ + CySA+), CNVP (Security+ + PenTest+), then the expert tiers.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **CySA+ (CS0-003)** — The defender's exam: can you work a security operations shift? Domain weights: Security Operations 34%, Vulnerability Management 26%, Incident Response 24%, Reporting and Communication 16%. The exam thinks in workflows, not definitions.
- **Vulnerability management lifecycle** — Discover → prioritize → remediate/mitigate → verify → report. Prioritization is the tested skill: a critical CVE on an isolated test box loses to a high CVE on an internet-facing production server.
- **CVSS triage formula** — CVSS severity × asset criticality × threat intel (exploitability). Context beats the raw score every time.
- **SIEM correlation** — Security Information and Event Management: correlation rules, timeline building, distinguishing true positives from noise. Practice reading firewall, IDS, and endpoint logs as narratives.
- **Incident response phases** — Preparation → detection/analysis → containment → eradication → recovery → lessons learned. Know what belongs in each phase and what the *first* action is: contain, don't eradicate, when the scope is unknown.
- **AI in security operations** — Now an explicit topic: know where ML helps (anomaly detection, alert triage) and where it doesn't (final attribution, legal judgment).
- **PenTest+ (PT0-003)** — The methodical offensive cert. Domain weights: Planning/Scoping 13%, Reconnaissance & Enumeration 21%, Attacks & Exploits 35%, Post-Exploitation 14%, Reporting 17%. The largest domain is attacks — but scoping and rules of engagement gate everything.
- **Recon: passive before active** — Passive recon (OSINT, DNS, WHOIS, certificate transparency) precedes active recon (scanning, enumeration). Know which techniques and tools fit which phase and what each reveals.
- **Post-exploitation discipline** — Persistence, lateral movement, pivoting, covering tracks — and the discipline of staying in scope while doing it.
- **Pentest reporting** — 17% of PenTest+ and the most under-studied: findings need severity, evidence, business impact, and remediation. A finding without remediation guidance is an incomplete finding.
- **SecurityX (X0-007, formerly CASP+)** — Expert tier: scenario-based and pass/fail. Domain weights: GRC 20%, Security Architecture 27%, Security Engineering 31%, Security Operations 22%. Questions present enterprise situations with competing constraints — budget, compliance, legacy systems.
- **Trade-off reasoning** — Every control has a cost (money, usability, performance). The right answer balances the constraint set, not the ideal. Architecture answers must cite the governing GRC requirement.
- **CSAP** — CompTIA Security Analytics Professional stackable: Security+ + CySA+.
- **CNVP** — CompTIA Network Vulnerability Assessment Professional stackable: Security+ + PenTest+.
- **CSAE / CSIE** — The expert-tier stackables that cap the security track after SecurityX.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Two drills, one per posture — defender and attacker. Run the defender drill daily; run the attacker drill as a weekly engagement simulation.

**Defender drill — the SOC shift (CySA+):**
1. **Ingest the alert.** Take one SIEM alert (or write one: source IP, destination, port, action, timestamp). Read it as a narrative, not a data point.
2. **Correlate.** Build the timeline: what happened before and after? One alert is noise; three correlated alerts are a story.
3. **Classify and prioritize.** Apply the triage formula: CVSS severity × asset criticality × threat intel. Score three findings and rank them — defend the ranking out loud.
4. **Respond by phase.** Name the incident-response phase and the first action. Unknown scope → contain first, eradicate later. Write the containment step as an imperative sentence.
5. **Report.** Draft the finding: severity, evidence, business impact, remediation. If any of the four is missing, the finding is incomplete.

**Attacker drill — the engagement walkthrough (PenTest+):**
1. **Scope.** Write the rules of engagement for a fictional target: in-scope hosts, forbidden techniques, time window, reporting contact. Nothing proceeds without this page.
2. **Recon.** List passive sources first (DNS, WHOIS, certificate transparency, OSINT), then active techniques (scanning, enumeration) — and what each reveals.
3. **Attack.** Match the technique to the target surface: network, wireless, application, cloud. For each technique, state the *why* (e.g., why LLMNR poisoning works: legacy name resolution trusting unauthenticated responses).
4. **Post-exploit.** Enumerate persistence, lateral movement, pivoting — and recheck scope at every step.
5. **Report.** Same four-element finding as the defender drill. The attacker and defender write the same report; only the perspective differs.

notes.body:

Write the timeline, the triage ranking of three findings using the CVSS × criticality × threat-intel formula, and the first three actions with their incident-response phases named.
- Scoping memo: rules of engagement for a penetration test of the same fictional company's public web application — in-scope hosts, forbidden techniques, time window, emergency contact, reporting cadence. Then the finding template: severity, evidence, business impact, remediation.
- Stackable map: Security+ → CySA+ → CSAP; Security+ → PenTest+ → CNVP; the path to SecurityX and the expert stackables — with current domain weights cited for each.

Deliverable: the tabletop packet plus the scoping memo. Original scenarios only — nothing here is recalled exam content.

modules.title: CompTIA Data & Cloud: Cloud+, Linux+, Server+, Data+, DataSys+, Project+
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3 of IL-09, the Adaptive Certification Command. I'm your instructor, and this module is the infrastructure and data expansion: Cloud+ (the vendor-neutral multi-cloud operator), Linux+ (the OS that runs the world's servers), Server+ (the hardware and datacenter beneath it), Data+ and DataSys+ (the data layer), and Project+ (leading the work). Cloud+ assumes you can already think in cloud, then tests whether you can run it — and the single most-tested concept is the shared responsibility model. Linux+ rewards systemd fluency and declarative automation thinking; Server+ rewards the failure math of RAID and the two numbers every disaster-recovery question reduces to — RTO and RPO. Data+ walks the full lifecycle from concepts to governance, and this module cross-links to IL-04's Linux path, IL-05's platform work, and IL-07's data spine: one discipline per topic, examined here.
objectives: Distinguish the Cloud+ domains: architecture, deployment, operations, security, DevOps fundamentals.
Reach Linux+ system-management fluency: services, users, security, automation, troubleshooting.
Cover Server+ hardware and disaster-recovery with datacenter realism.
Work the Data+/DataSys+ data lifecycle: concepts → acquisition → analysis → governance.
Use Project+ to formalize leading technical work.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Cloud+ (CV0-004)** — The vendor-neutral cloud operator cert. Domain weights: Cloud Architecture 23%, Deployment 19%, Operations 17%, Security 19%, DevOps Fundamentals 10%, Troubleshooting 12%. It tests whether you can *run* cloud, not whether you can recite vendor syntax.
- **Shared responsibility model** — The single most-tested cloud concept: know exactly where the provider's duty ends and yours begins. Under IaaS, the provider secures *of* the cloud (hypervisor, physical); you patch the guest OS.
- **Six R's of migration** — Rehost, Replatform, Repurchase, Refactor/Re-architect, Retain, Retire. Know when each fits: only refactor/re-architect changes the application architecture.
- **Linux+ (XK0-006)** — System Management 23%, Services/User Management 20%, Security 18%, Automation 17%, Troubleshooting 22%. The OS exam for the OS that runs the world's servers.
- **systemd fluency** — Units, targets, journalctl: `journalctl -u <service>` is the first stop when a service fails. Know permissions/ACLs, LVM/storage, package management, shell scripting basics, containers at concept level.
- **Declarative automation** — The modern 17%: Ansible-style declarative thinking, cron/systemd timers, scripted remediation. Automation 17% is where Linux+ separates from a trivia exam.
- **Server+ (SK0-005)** — The hardware and datacenter: Installation 18%, Administration 30%, Security/DR 24%, Troubleshooting 28%. Datacenter realism: power/cooling, physical security, backup types.
- **RAID failure math** — RAID 0/1/5/6/10 trade-offs: know what each survives. RAID 10 (mirror+stripe): fast, survives multi-disk failure in different mirrors, 50% capacity overhead. Know the failure math cold.
- **RTO vs RPO** — Recovery Time Objective (how fast systems return) vs Recovery Point Objective (how much data loss is tolerable). Every DR question reduces to these two numbers. RPO of 4 hours means backups at least every 4 hours.
- **Backup types** — Full, incremental, differential: differential = all changes since last full, so one differential suffices at restore time — faster restore, larger backup.
- **Data+ (DA0-002)** — Data Concepts 20%, Acquisition/Preparation 22%, Analysis 24%, Visualization 20%, Governance 14%. The full data lifecycle.
- **Data quality dimensions** — Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness (validity and uniqueness often listed too).
- **ETL vs ELT** — Extract-Transform-Load vs Extract-Load-Transform: where the transformation happens changes cost, latency, and governance.
- **Chart selection** — Trend over time → line chart; composition → stacked bar; distribution → histogram. A line chart answers the 12-month trend question; a pie chart answers single-point composition.
- **Correlation vs causation** — Correlation is co-movement; causation needs mechanism plus controlled evidence. Never infer cause from a correlation coefficient.
- **DataSys+ (DS0-001)** — Database administration depth and data integration: normalization forms, indexing strategy, backup/recovery for databases, integration patterns.
- **Project+ (PK0-005)** — Formalizes running technical work: project basics, the constraints (scope/time/cost/quality), communication, change control. The vocabulary of leading without authority.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The operator's drill sequence — one procedure per layer, run until each is reflex.

1. **Shared-responsibility triage.** Take any cloud scenario and draw the line: provider duties vs your duties, for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. If you can't place the line, you can't answer Cloud+'s security questions.
2. **Migration-strategy matching.** For each workload in a fictional estate (legacy monolith, commodity web app, end-of-life tool), choose one of the six R's and defend it. Only refactor changes the architecture — name what changes.
3. **systemd rescue drill.** Given a failed service: `systemctl status`, then `journalctl -u <service>` to read the failure, then fix and restart. Time yourself; the first stop is always the journal.
4. **RAID failure-math drill.** State the capacity overhead and survivable failure for RAID 1, 5, 6, 10 from memory. Then: which survives two disk failures in the same array? (RAID 6; RAID 10 only if in different mirrors.)
5. **RTO/RPO worked estimation.** A business says: "We can lose at most 4 hours of data and must be back in 24 hours." Write: RPO = 4h → backup cadence ≤ 4h. RTO = 24h → restore must complete in 24h → differential beats incremental at restore time (one differential suffices). Show the arithmetic.
6. **Chart-selection drill.** Given a message (trend, composition, distribution), pick the chart and defend it. Then name what makes a dashboard honest: labeled axes, zero baselines, no cherry-picked ranges.
7. **Data lifecycle walkthrough.** Take one dataset and walk it: concepts → acquisition/preparation → analysis → visualization → governance. At each stage name the quality dimension and the governance control.

modules.title: Oracle: Java, SQL, and OCI
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 5 of IL-09, the Adaptive Certification Command. I'm your instructor, and this module is Oracle's three certification families: Java SE (the language credential — streams, lambdas, modules, virtual threads), Database SQL (queries through DDL/DML), and OCI (the year-versioned cloud program from Foundations to Professional). The official objectives are the topic maps; original code practice is the preparation. Java's 1Z0-830 is 50 questions in 120 minutes at a 68% pass mark — and it loves compilation-failure questions, so you learn to read for what won't compile before evaluating what it prints. Oracle SQL's 1Z0-071 is 63 questions in 120 minutes at 63% — pure SQL fluency under time pressure. And OCI carries year versions (like 1Z0-1085-26): the Foundations exam is free, 40 questions in 60 minutes at 65%, and compartments are the identity boundary every IAM question reduces to.
objectives: Master Java SE 21 exam topics: streams, lambdas, modules, concurrency with virtual threads, I/O, generics.

Apply Oracle's exam mechanics: question counts, timing, and pass marks per exam.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **1Z0-830 (Java SE 21 Developer)** — 50 questions, 120 minutes, 68% to pass. The exam tests precise language semantics — code-reading under time pressure. Pacing: 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4 minutes per question; anything that eats more gets flagged.
- **Stream laziness** — Intermediate operations (filter, map, peek) do nothing until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce) executes. Trace stream pipelines mentally, watching for laziness.
- **Collectors & Optionals** — The stream pipeline's finishers: collectors aggregate, Optionals force explicit empty-handling. Know intermediate vs terminal by sight.
- **JPMS (Java Platform Module System)** — module-info.java, requires/exports/opens: know what breaks when a package isn't exported.
- **Virtual threads (Project Loom)** — Thread-per-task becomes viable at scale for I/O-bound work; watch for synchronized blocks pinning carrier threads. Structured concurrency concepts are in scope.
- **PECS** — Producer Extends, Consumer Super: `? extends T` when reading (producer), `? super T` when writing (consumer). Know the type-erasure consequences behind it.
- **NIO.2** — Path/Files APIs, try-with-resources, serialization basics; localization: Locale, ResourceBundle, formatting.
- **Compilation-failure tactic** — The exam's favorite trap: read for what won't compile before evaluating what it prints.
- **1Z0-071 (Oracle Database SQL)** — 63 questions, 120 minutes, 63% to pass. Pure SQL fluency: queries, joins, subqueries, DDL, DML, transaction control.
- **Join-condition vs filter trap** — Filtering the nullable side of an outer join in WHERE converts it to an inner join. Put the filter in the ON clause or lose the outer semantics — a classic trap.
- **Subquery operators** — Single-row (`=`, `<`, `>`) vs multi-row (`IN`, `ANY`, `ALL`); correlated subqueries; EXISTS vs IN (EXISTS stops at the first match and handles NULL semantics cleanly).
- **Set operators** — UNION (distinct) vs UNION ALL (straight concatenation, faster), INTERSECT, MINUS: column count and type compatibility rules.
- **Constraints** — PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL on CREATE/ALTER; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, MERGE; transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT).
- **1Z0-171 (Oracle 23ai SQL Associate)** — The newer SQL track. Check which your target role expects before booking 1Z0-071.
- **OCI year-versioning** — OCI certifications carry year versions (e.g., 1Z0-1085-26). Objectives refresh annually: study the current year's guide and schedule before your version retires.
- **OCI Foundations (1Z0-1085)** — 40 questions, 60 minutes, 65% to pass — and the exam itself is free. Domains: core services 50% (compute, storage, networking, databases), security 25% (IAM, compartments, encryption), governance 10%. The cheapest credential in enterprise cloud.
- **Compartments** — The OCI identity boundary: every IAM question reduces to compartment + policy syntax. Policies attach at compartment scope.
- **OCI Professional tracks** — Architect Associate (1Z0-1072): design for HA across availability/fault domains, VCN design, load balancing, data services selection; plus Developer, DevOps, Networking, Security Professional paths.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The code-tracing drill — language exams are precision instruments, so the preparation is tracing, not reading.

1. **Work the pacing math.** Java: 120 minutes ÷ 50 questions = 2.4 min/question. SQL: 120 ÷ 63 ≈ 1.9 min/question. OCI Foundations: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 min/question. Write your per-question budget on the runbook card; anything that eats double gets flagged.
2. **Compilation first.** For every Java snippet: decide compile-or-not before deciding output. The exam loves compilation-failure questions — read for what won't compile first.
3. **Trace by hand.** Write the output on paper before checking: stream pipelines (watch laziness), generics bounds (PECS), try-with-resources closure order. The gap between your trace and the real output is the lesson.
4. **Drill the SQL traps.** Outer-join + WHERE filter (the semantics killer), EXISTS vs IN with NULLs, UNION vs UNION ALL. Write ten of each by hand; speed comes from reps.
5. **Draw the OCI boundary.** For every IAM scenario: name the compartment, write the policy in compartment + resource + action form. If you can't state the boundary, you can't answer the question.
6. **Year-version check.** Before studying OCI: confirm the current year's guide, and schedule before your version retires. Studying a retired year's objectives is donated effort.
7. **Trap log.** Keep a personal log: mutable defaults, PECS direction mistakes, the joins you misread. Review it before every practice set.

The official objectives are the topic maps; this procedure is the preparation.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **HFCP (Hyperledger Fabric Certified Practitioner)** — 90-minute online proctored multiple-choice. Domains: Fabric Networks 36%, Smart Contracts 24%, Client Applications 24%, plus fundamentals.
- **Permissioned ledger** — Fabric's identity-first model: organizations, MSPs, and channels before anything else. Identity and channels first, tokens never.
- **Peers** — Endorse transactions (execute chaincode) and commit blocks to the ledger.
- **Orderers** — Run the consensus service (Raft) and cut blocks. In Fabric, orderers order; peers endorse and commit — never mix the roles.
- **Channels** — Private subnets of the ledger: only member organizations see a channel's data.
- **Organizations / MSPs** — Membership Service Providers: the identity layer that decides who belongs to the network.
- **Transaction flow** — Propose → endorse (chaincode execution) → order → validate → commit. Know which node does what at each step.
- **Chaincode lifecycle** — Package → install → approve (per organization) → commit (channel). The governance is the point: no single org can deploy unilaterally.
- **Client applications** — Fabric SDKs, the Gateway service, submitting vs evaluating transactions; private data collections for selective privacy.
- **LFS272** — The LF's own Fabric course material: aligned prep, but study the current exam domains, not any single course's table of contents.
- **BCP (Besu Certified Professional)** — 90-minute online proctored multiple-choice; two attempts included; valid 2 years. Domains: Networking 26%, Core Concepts 24%, then permissioning, privacy, consensus.
- **Ethereum client** — Besu is an Ethereum client for permissioned networks: EVM compatibility means Solidity and standard tooling transfer.
- **Node discovery** — discv4/dns discovery, bootnodes, static nodes: how a permissioned network actually forms.
- **Permissioning** — Node and account permissioning via on-chain contracts: who may join, who may transact.
- **Tessera / privacy groups** — Private transactions: private payloads alongside public state — the enterprise privacy pattern.
- **QBFT/IBFT vs Ethash** — Proof-of-authority BFT consensus (immediate finality, no mining) vs proof-of-work. Know the finality and fault-tolerance trade-offs.
- **Two-attempt strategy** — Two attempts included changes strategy: sit the first as a calibrated diagnostic if you're borderline-ready.
- **Retired: CHFA/CHFD/CHSA** — The old performance-based exams are gone, along with the Sawtooth curriculum (LFS273/LFD272). Do not build study plans on these.
- **Verification habit** — Before starting ANY certification, confirm it exists on the issuer's site today. Programs sunset quietly.
- **Systems-operations lens** — Taught with a blockchain engineer's lens: the exam tests whether you can run the network, not whether you can hype it.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The systems-operator's study sequence — learn each network as a machine you will run, not a whitepaper you will quote.

**HFCP sequence:**
1. **Draw the network.** Three orgs, two channels, peers and an ordering service. Label every node with its role: endorse, order, commit. If you can't draw it, you don't know it.
2. **Walk a transaction.** Propose → endorse → order → validate → commit. At each step, name the node type acting and the artifact it produces.
3. **Run the chaincode lifecycle.** Package → install → approve (per org) → commit (channel). Say out loud why approval is per-organization — the governance is the point.
4. **Submit vs evaluate.** Write the difference: evaluation reads, submission writes. Private data collections: who sees what.
5. **Domain-weight the reps.** Fabric Networks 36% gets the most hours; fundamentals get the fewest. Study by weight.

**BCP sequence:**
1. **Form the network.** Bootnodes, static nodes, discovery (discv4/dns): narrate how a permissioned network bootstraps from zero.
2. **Permission it.** Node permissioning, account permissioning: who may join, who may transact — and the on-chain contracts that enforce it.
3. **Make it private.** Tessera/privacy groups: draw public state vs private payload. Know the enterprise pattern by heart.
4. **Choose consensus.** QBFT/IBFT vs Ethash: finality and fault-tolerance trade-offs, stated as engineering decisions.
5. **Use the two attempts.** Borderline-ready? Sit attempt one as a calibrated diagnostic, then close the gaps and sit attempt two. The format is part of the strategy.

**Both:** verify the exam exists on the LF site before starting. Retired objectives are the most expensive mistake in certification.

modules.title: C++ and Python Institute Certifications
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 7 of IL-09, the Adaptive Certification Command. I'm your instructor, and this module is the language-vendor credentials: the C++ Institute's CPE → CPA → CPP ladder (plus the C branch: CLE/CLA/CLP) and the Python Institute's PCEP → PCAP → PCPP1 → PCPP2 ladder, with OpenEDG's free aligned courses as the study backbone. Language exams test precision — one character changes the answer — so this module trains the precision habit: trace every snippet by hand, write the output before checking, and keep a trap log. CPE-20-01 is entry at 70% to pass, CPA-21-02 is the associate depth (OOP, STL, templates basics, exceptions), CPP-22-02 is professional. On the Python side, PCEP is the vocabulary, PCAP-31-03 is the associate (modules, OOP, exceptions, generators, closures, decorators), and PCPP1/PCPP2 are the professional tiers. The exam style is predict-the-output with subtle distractors — mutable default args, late-binding closures, the most vexing parse. This module is the credential map and the exam-tactic layer over IL-03's programming depth.
objectives: Climb the C++ ladder: CPE (entry) → CPA (associate) → CPP (professional).
Climb the Python ladder: PCEP (entry) → PCAP (associate) → PCPP1/PCPP2 (professional).

Develop exam precision: trace code, predict output, spot the compilation failure.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **CPE-20-01** — C++ Certified Entry-Level Programmer: entry rung, 70% to pass. Basics: types, operators, control flow, functions, pointers at introduction level.
- **CPA-21-02** — C++ Certified Associate Programmer: the associate depth — OOP (classes, inheritance, polymorphism, virtual), templates basics, STL containers/algorithms, exception handling.
- **CPP-22-02** — C++ Certified Professional Programmer: professional tier — advanced templates, STL mastery, concurrency basics, idioms and best practices.
- **CLE / CLA / CLP** — The C branch mirroring the ladder for C itself: entry, associate, professional. Useful for embedded/systems roles where C++ is overkill.
- **Most vexing parse** — `Widget w();` declares a FUNCTION, not an object. Use `Widget w{};` or `Widget w;`. The exam's favorite C++ declaration trap.
- **Undefined behavior** — Sequence-point and lifetime rules: UB questions punish guessers. Know the rules cold; never reason from "it worked on my machine."
- **PCEP** — Python Certified Entry-Level Programmer: the vocabulary of Python — literals, operators, control flow, functions, basic data structures.
- **PCAP-31-03** — Python Certified Associate Programmer: modules/packages, OOP, exceptions, string and file processing, generators/closures/decorators at associate depth.
- **PCPP1** — Professional tier 1: advanced OOP (metaclasses, descriptors), networking (sockets), GUI basics, design patterns in Python.
- **PCPP2** — Professional tier 2: file processing depth, database/SQLite, numerical/scientific basics, best practices and PEP conventions.
- **OpenEDG** — Publishes free courses aligned to each Python Institute and C++ Institute exam: the legitimate study backbone. Sufficient alongside the official exam syllabi.
- **Mutable default argument** — `def f(x=[]):` — the list is created ONCE at def time; mutations persist across calls. The classic Python trap.
- **Late-binding closures** — Loop variables bind late in lambdas: `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` gives three functions that all see the final value 2. Capture with a default argument.
- **Integer caching** — CPython caches small ints (−5..256): identity comparisons on them can surprise. Know the range; never rely on `is` for value equality.
- **Trap log** — Your personal ledger of every trap that caught you: mutable defaults, except-clause ordering, most-vexing-parse, dangling references, late binding. Reviewed before every practice set.
- **Precision habit** — Language exams are precision instruments: the preparation is tracing, not reading.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The precision-tracing drill — the only procedure that works on predict-the-output exams.

1. **Read the snippet twice.** First pass: what does it claim to do. Second pass: character by character — the exam's distractors live in single characters (`[]` vs `()`, `is` vs `==`, `w()` vs `w{}`).
2. **Classify the trap family.** Is it a lifetime trap (dangling reference, mutable default)? A binding trap (late-binding closure, PECS direction)? A parse trap (most vexing parse)? Naming the family routes you to the rule.
3. **Write the output before checking.** On paper, not in your head: the exact output, or "compilation failure" / exception type with the line. The gap between your trace and reality is the lesson.
4. **Trace the machine, not the intent.** For C++: object lifetimes, sequence points, overload resolution. For Python: name resolution order, evaluation time of defaults, closure cell contents.
5. **Log every miss.** Each wrong trace goes in the trap log with the rule restated in your own words. The log is reviewed before every practice set — it is the highest-value study artifact you own.
6. **Run the OpenEDG labs.** The free aligned courses include exercises: do them from the starter, not by reading the solution. Code you typed teaches; code you read doesn't.
7. **Gate by ladder rung.** PCEP before PCAP, CPA before CPP. Each rung's practice set at 80%+ twice before the voucher is bought.

Cross-link: IL-03's Programming Backbone is the deep study behind these exams — this module is the credential map and the exam-tactic layer.

scriptLabs.title: Subnet Sprint: /26 in 60 Seconds
scriptLabs.brief: Build a subnet calculator drill function: given a CIDR like 192.168.10.0/26, print network, broadcast, first/last usable, and host count. The required fragments force the bit-math, not a library call.
scriptLabs.starter:
def subnet_info(cidr):
    # parse 'a.b.c.d/n', compute network/broadcast/usable range by hand
    pass

print(subnet_info('192.168.10.0/26'))
scriptLabs.hint: host_bits = 32 - prefix. mask = (0xFFFFFFFF << host_bits) & 0xFFFFFFFF. network = ip & mask; broadcast = network | ~mask.
scriptLabs.solution:
def subnet_info(cidr):
    addr, pfx = cidr.split('/')
    pfx = int(pfx)
    octs = [int(x) for x in addr.split('.')]
    ip = (octs[0]<<24)|(octs[1]<<16)|(octs[2]<<8)|octs[3]
    hb = 32 - pfx
    mask = (0xFFFFFFFF << hb) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    net = ip & mask
    bcast = net | (0xFFFFFFFF ^ mask)
    hosts = (1 << hb) - 2
    f = lambda n: '.'.join(str((n >> s) & 255) for s in (24,16,8,0))
    out = f'net={f(net)} bcast={f(bcast)} usable={f(net+1)}-{f(bcast-1)} hosts={hosts}'
    print(out)
    return out

subnet_info('192.168.10.0/26')

scriptLabs.title: SQL Outer-Join Trap: ON vs WHERE
scriptLabs.brief: Write two queries against a customers/orders schema: one filtering the nullable side in WHERE (the trap), one in ON (correct). Show how the first silently becomes an inner join.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- schema: customers(id, name), orders(id, customer_id, total)
-- Q1 (trap): LEFT JOIN with filter in WHERE
-- Q2 (correct): LEFT JOIN with filter in ON
scriptLabs.hint: WHERE total > 100 after a LEFT JOIN removes the NULL-extended rows — the outer join collapses to inner.
scriptLabs.solution:
-- Q1 TRAP: filter in WHERE collapses the outer join
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 100;  -- NULL rows (no orders) are removed -> effectively INNER

-- Q2 CORRECT: filter in ON preserves all customers
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 100;  -- customers with no big orders still appear (NULL)

options.why: Freshness without remediation repeats the result — and burns the retake fee.

options.text: Rebook — the gap log is closed

options.text: Study two more months to be safe

options.text: Rebook without retesting the weak domain

steps.prompt: How do you allocate the final week's hours?

options.text: Weight hours to Automation and Troubleshooting gaps; maintain System Management with light drills

options.text: Only practice your strongest domain for confidence
options.why: Confidence in strong domains doesn't move the score; closing gaps does.

answerBank.q: In what order should I take A+, Network+, Security+?
answerBank.a: A+ → Network+ → Security+. The knowledge compounds (hardware/OS → networking → security lens), and the order earns CIOS then CSIS stackables with no wasted exams.

answerBank.q: How do I prepare for PBQs without braindumps?
answerBank.a: Hands-on labs and simulations only. PBQs test applied skill — build/troubleshoot real systems (or faithful simulations) until the workflows are reflex. Memorizing recalled questions is both unethical and ineffective, since PBQ pools rotate.
Security+ first, always. CySA+ assumes the Security+ vocabulary and adds the operations workflow (SIEM, vuln management, IR). Skipping the base makes CySA+ twice as hard.

answerBank.q: How do I choose between Cloud+, Linux+, Server+?
answerBank.a: By role target: cloud operations → Cloud+; Linux administration → Linux+; datacenter/hardware → Server+. They overlap ~30% — take the one matching your next job, then add the second; the marginal study cost is low.

answerBank.q: Are vendor AI badges worth it?
answerBank.a: As learning proof, yes; as hiring signal, proctored exams beat badges. Do the badge for the skill, sit the proctored exam for the signal — and never build a plan on a pilot program.

answerBank.q: Which Oracle cert first: Java, SQL, or OCI?
answerBank.a: SQL first if you're data-bound (fastest win), Java if you're a developer (deepest), OCI Foundations if you're cloud-bound (free exam, fastest credential). The three don't overlap — pick by vector.

answerBank.q: HFCP or BCP — which blockchain cert?
answerBank.a: HFCP if you operate permissioned Fabric networks (enterprise/consortium); BCP if you work the Ethereum-compatible Besu stack. Both are 90-minute proctored multiple-choice. Confirm both are still live on the LF site before starting.

answerBank.q: PCEP → PCAP → PCPP: how long between?
answerBank.a: PCEP to PCAP: 2–4 months of steady study. PCAP to PCPP1: 4–6 months — the jump is real (metaclasses, networking, patterns). Use OpenEDG's free aligned courses throughout.
